extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants working on alloys, polymers, polymer compositions, textile- and fiber-related inventions (materials/chemistry domain)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and drafting of patent applications in materials fields (alloys, polymers, polymer compositions, textiles), covering requirements for description, claims, novelty (identity), and inventive step with illustrative examples and notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for amended numerical ranges / added matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment that reduces or alters a numerical limitation (e.g., changing an upper limit) is allowable provided the amended numerical range is included in the matter stated in the original specification (e.g., by specific embodiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Original range 200–10000 μm amended to 200–6000 μm is acceptable if the original specification disclosed ranges or embodiments that make the amended upper limit (6000 μm) already specified or appropriately included in the original disclosure; thus the amendment does not add new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity criterion for alloy inventions (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of an alloy invention is determined by whether each element of the alloy is identical and whether its composition range, structure, and utility (property or use) are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: For alloy inventions, utility that limits a specific composition or structure should be construed as specifying the alloy. For manufacturing-method claims, identity requires considering identity of both the alloy and the manufacturing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine identity — same composition & structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed and prior-art alloys have identical composition and structure, they are substantially identical even if perceived properties or uses differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the prior art does not explicitly disclose a use, the composition and structure appropriate to that use may already be present; differences that are merely differences in stated use do not establish novelty. (See cited case law examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine identity — composition identical but structure depends on manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: If alloy compositions are identical but structure depends on manufacturing method, identity must consider whether the same manufacturing method is applied; same composition plus same method => substantially identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure of an alloy commonly changes with manufacturing; where prior art and claim share both composition and manufacturing method, inventions are substantially identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine identity — identical composition but different structure/property/use
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with identical compositions, if structures, properties or uses are different (e.g., microstructures conferring different functions), the inventions may be different (novel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Two Fe alloys with same composition but different micro-lamellar structure leading to different suitability (piano wire vs cogwheel) are different inventions when specification and knowledge at filing indicate distinct structures and functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to determine identity — different perceived properties within same use scope
rubrics_metrics.description: If perceived differences in properties do not produce a new use but are included in the existing utility, the property is inherent and the inventions are substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Two alloy disclosures with overlapping composition ranges and essentially the same properties and uses (heat resisting vs electrical resistance material) are substantially identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for alloy inventions — factors to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine inventive step for an alloy invention, consider alloy composition and necessary structure; the utility of the alloy (specific property or use); and specific means (manufacturing method) to obtain the structure or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All these elements (composition, structure, utility, method) should be weighed together when assessing obviousness/inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-step rule — mere composition-range changes or substitutions are not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing to a known alloy with the same base, an alloy differing only by (i) a different composition range, (ii) an additional alloying element, or (iii) substitution by another alloying element does not involve inventive step unless the claimed alloy shows significantly improved utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: If known alloy has 3–8% A, claimed 1–2% or 9–15% A (same objective/property) corresponds to (i); adding 0.05–0.5% B corresponds to (ii); substituting one element by another with known equivalent effect corresponds to (iii). Such differences are typically obvious absent significant improvement in utility. Case law and notes show overlap/impurities often negate novelty/inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-step rule — different structure or utility may support inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alloy has a different structure or utility (e.g., different properties arising from manufacturing) compared to prior art, that difference may support inventive step; but if structure/utility is similar when composition and manufacturing method are similar, no inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because structure depends on manufacturing, overlapping composition ranges can correspond to identical utility unless manufacturing conditions meaningfully differ. Claims asserting structural differences must provide evidence (effects/tests) showing practical, non-trivial difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description requirement for polymeric compounds — sufficiency and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular polymeric compound must be described with specific explanation sufficient to support the polymer defined in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, specify the polymer by structure via: repeating units; arrangement of repeating units (homo, random, block, graft, head-to-tail coupling, etc.); molecular weight; local molecular properties (branching, substituents, double bonds, cross-linking, terminal groups); and stereospecificity (atactic, isotactic, syndiotactic). If complete specification is impossible, clearly specify main components and relevant structural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative specification for polymers — quantitative basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If structure-based specification is difficult, specify other requirements representing basic properties in a quantitative manner (e.g., viscosity, crystallinity, Tg, melting point, density, tensile strength, elongation, modulus, hardness, impact strength, transparency, refractive index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic property requirements must be quantitative and measured by commonly used methods; if atypical methods are used, describe them specifically so a skilled person can reproduce measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing method as part of polymer specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If structure and basic properties are insufficient to specify the polymer, include the manufacturing method as part of the specification to more clearly define the polymeric compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing details help when the polymer is a distribution of molecules; include source materials, conditions, and devices where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification data for polymers — proof of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific identification data proving the existence of the polymeric compound so a person skilled in the art can readily recognize it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: elemental analysis, chemical-bond analysis, Tg, refractive index, molecular weight, melting point, viscosity, IR spectrum, physical properties. Measurement methods must be described and be commonly used or specifically explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose manufacturing methods (polymers) — at least one or more
rubrics_metrics.description: To enable a skilled person to synthesize the claimed polymeric compound, describe at least more than one manufacturing method with essential matters such as source materials, manufacturing conditions, and, if necessary, manufacturing devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and specific numerical values and operating conditions should be provided so the skilled person can carry out the process without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim defines a use of a polymer, provide examples proving applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a use of a polymeric compound is defined in the claim, the description must specifically describe at least one example proving that the claimed polymer is applicable for that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical demonstration in the specification supports utility and claim support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing-method invention (polymers) — three essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention on a manufacturing method of polymeric compounds must comprise three essential elements: (a) source materials, (b) processing means, and (c) expected products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) New source compounds require specific manufacturing description. (b) Processing means (solvents, catalysts, temperature, pressure, time, etc.) must be clearly and specifically described; examples with numerical values should be given. (c) If product is a new polymer, specifically identify it and state more than one physical/chemical property proving existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymer composition description requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A polymer composition invention must describe matters related to the composition itself and its use, including source materials and mixing ratios, special features of state or property, embodiments with specific numerical values, and manufacturing methods for any new starting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must state which property is improved or newly obtained and must state at least one use to prove utility. Utility is properly stated when application to a specific use is objectively described, properties clearly show the use, or the use is obvious from objectives and technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — polymers and polymer compositions (definitional principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for polymeric compounds should particularly define the polymer sought for protection, preferably by structure; if structure is insufficient, add basic properties or manufacturing method. For manufacturing-method claims, define the three essential elements and their technical relationship. For polymer compositions, components and mixing ratio should be clearly defined; if function/use limitation is claimed, define that function/use in addition to components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claim language (e.g., 'composition having a function of XX') is appropriate when component limits alone do not distinguish the invention from other compositions lacking the function; otherwise component limits suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile description requirements — chemical fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions relating to chemical fibers characterized by material properties, applicants must specifically state technical means including source material, structural characteristics of the fiber, process conditions (spinning, drawing, post-treatment) to accomplish the claimed characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a skilled person would need excessive repeated testing or trial-and-error due to lack of clear description of means, the description is insufficient for enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile description requirements — textile structures (fabric/knit)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions relating to textile structure, where the structure is not a basic structure readily recognizable to a skilled person, applicants must specifically state complete characteristics of the structure including repeating unit and manufacturing methods in the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed structural and manufacturing disclosures are required to enable reproduction and to delimit the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-step consideration — fibers from known linear polymers
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention using a linear polymer generally known to the public for simple manufacturing of fiber without other distinctive characteristics is deemed to have no inventive step unless the invention has distinctive characteristics and utility not expected from the known polymer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive characteristics must be shown to be non-obvious and yield utility that cannot be expected from fibers made from the publicly known polymer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-step consideration — parameter-based claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim specifies a new parameter for man-made fiber, it is necessary to compare the manufacturing method and material properties (e.g., strength) with prior art to determine inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses process variables that determine the parameter and values convert into the claimed parameter range, the parameter may be obvious. Examples show parameters that merely describe inherent properties are not patentable when predictable from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims specifying spinning/manufacturing method — claim scope construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When construing claims relating to fiber material specified by a spinning/manufacturing method, the claim should not be limited to embodiments in the description but should include the whole span of properties producible by the claimed method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examples and comparative examples show meaningful differences in technical characteristics attributable to the method, novelty and inventive step may be recognized; but claim breadth should reflect the full range of properties the method can produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile design features — subjective evaluation and technical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Textile inventions with design features are evaluated subjectively for exterior beauty; if the structure or process is obvious to a skilled person or is disclosed in prior art, the invention lacks inventive step; however, if the design structure has a new technical function, patentability can be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design contributions that produce technical effects beyond appearance can support patentability; mere aesthetic differences that are obvious do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect from limited/minute shape differences — need for data
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute shape differences of components (ring, traveler, metal card clothing, knitting needle, etc.) may greatly influence results; the examiner must consider the effect of small shape changes and, where doubtful, require test data or certified test results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When effect is uncertain, objective evidence (tests, certified results) should be used to support claimed effects of shape differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of textile inventions related to traditional art — search non-patent literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications related to traditional art (passed from masters to pupils) often cannot be examined precisely by patent document search alone; examiners should search non-patent documents to determine inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., natural dyeing methods may require historical, regional, or other non-patent sources to assess prior knowledge and inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of related technical fields for textile machinery — expand prior-art search
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining inventive step of textile machinery, expand the scope of prior-art search beyond the relevant IPC (D section) to general machinery fields; consider non-patent documents like device guidelines or catalogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textile machinery often draws on general machine engineering; examiners should consider well-known prior art in other technical fields and include non-patent literature submitted in examination or invalidation trials.
